opus-5.5.text:
I think the first thing to say is that MAD, the mechanistic architecture design suite, is really useful precisely because it breaks things down into small, synthetic tasks that each probe a specific capability. You have things like in-context recall, fuzzy recall, noisy recall, selective copying, compression, and memorization. Each one isolates something different. So I'd be a bit cautious about collapsing everything into one averaged number, because that can hide exactly the information the benchmark was designed to surface.

For example, a recurrent model or a linear attention variant might look great on memorization or compression, but struggle on in-context recall when you increase the number of key-value pairs or the sequence length. If you just average, you might conclude two architectures are roughly equivalent when in fact they have very different strengths. So I think reporting per-task performance, and ideally looking at how performance scales as you vary difficulty, like vocabulary size, sequence length, or the number of items to recall, is much more informative than a single score.

The second point is that these tasks are proxies. The original motivation was that performance on these small synthetic tasks correlates with scaling behavior and perplexity at larger scale, which makes them a cheap way to iterate on architecture design. But correlation isn't guarantee. So I see MAD as a diagnostic tool. It tells you where an architecture's memory or retrieval mechanism might break, and then you still need to validate at scale on language modeling, long-context benchmarks, needle-in-a-haystack style retrieval, and so on.

And third, especially for the kind of work we've been doing on memory, thinking about how models learn to memorize at test time, I think it's important to evaluate not only accuracy but how gracefully a model degrades. Does it fail catastrophically once its memory capacity is exceeded, or does it forget in a controlled way? That kind of question is something MAD-style tasks are really well suited to answer if you design the evaluation carefully, sweeping over capacity and interference rather than testing at a single fixed setting.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so the first thing I'd say is that MAD, the Mechanistic Architecture Design suite, is really a collection of small synthetic probes rather than one benchmark with one number. You've got in-context recall, fuzzy recall, noisy recall, selective copying, compression, memorization, and so on. Each of those was designed to isolate one capability that we think matters for sequence modeling, so the worst thing you can do is average them all together and call it a day. If you do that, an architecture that's great at compression and terrible at recall can look identical to one with the opposite profile, and those are completely different models from a practical standpoint.

So the way I think about it is more like a profile or a fingerprint. You look at the task-by-task breakdown and you ask, where does this architecture break? And more importantly, how does it break as you scale the difficulty? For recall tasks, that means sweeping the number of key-value pairs and the sequence length and watching when accuracy falls off a cliff. For a fixed-size recurrent state, you know there's a capacity limit, so the interesting question isn't whether it eventually fails, it's how gracefully it degrades and whether the state is being used efficiently. For Transformers, recall is basically free, but compression and memorization tell you something different about what they're actually learning.

The second thing is you have to control for the things that aren't architecture. Parameter count, state size, training budget, and especially hyperparameter sweeps. These tasks are small, so results can be very sensitive to learning rate and initialization, and I've seen cases where a model goes from near zero to near perfect just from a sweep. So the fair comparison is best-over-sweep for every model, at matched state size, otherwise you're measuring your tuning effort rather than the design.

And then the last point, which I think is the one people miss, is that MAD is a diagnostic, not a destination. Its value is in whether performance there predicts something at scale. So when we evaluate, we try to pair the MAD profile with at least one real language modeling or long-context result, and we ask whether the weaknesses we saw on the synthetic probes show up in the same places downstream. If they do, you've learned something transferable about the architecture. If they don't, that's also interesting, because it means the probe isn't capturing what you thought it was.

astra-6.text:
I think you want to look at the performance on each task separately, because the tasks are probing different capabilities. If you collapse everything into one average score, you can hide a weakness that might be very important for the application you care about.

And the comparison needs to be controlled. Are you comparing models with similar parameter counts and similar training budgets? Then you can ask how performance changes as you increase the difficulty of each task. A model might do well in an easy setting, but that doesn’t necessarily mean it has learned a solution that scales.

So I would treat MAD as a diagnostic: what is this architecture good at, where does it struggle, and what does that tell us about its design? Then you still need to test whether those findings carry over to the larger, real-world tasks you ultimately care about.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the important thing is to look at the tasks individually, because they’re testing different capabilities. If you collapse everything into one average score, you can hide the fact that a model is very good at one kind of task and struggles with another.

So I would look at the performance on each task, and then ask how that performance changes as you increase the sequence length or change the model’s capacity. And you want those comparisons to be under comparable training and compute budgets. That gives you a more useful picture of what an architecture can actually do, rather than just a single number that says one model is better.
